I honestly didn't expect the hike to take that long. We left the trailhead around seven, thinking we'd be back by noon, but the fog rolled in somewhere past the second ridge and everything slowed down. My boots were soaked through by the time we hit the switchbacks -- not fun, but kind of funny in hindsight.

There's this one spot, maybe a mile before the summit, where the trees just stop. No warning, no gradual thinning, just gone. You step out of the forest and suddenly you can see for miles, assuming the clouds cooperate, which ours did not. We sat there anyway, ate some very sad, very squashed sandwiches, and argued about whether it was worth pushing on.

It was. Barely. The summit itself was underwhelming -- a pile of rocks and a rusted sign nobody had bothered to replace since, I'd guess, the Clinton administration. But the way down was the real payoff. The fog broke right as we started descending, and for about twenty minutes the whole valley opened up gold and green like someone had flipped a switch. Nobody said much. What is there to say.

We got back to the car a little after four, tired, sunburned in weird patches, and immediately started planning the next one.
